subject: repairDroid
pitch:
Category: Humanoid character.
Subject: repair droid.
Style: Star Wars.
reasoning:
I'm designing a Star Wars-style bipedal repair droid with a boxy, weathered metal body, mismatched panels, a repair arm with tool attachments, a photoreceptor eye, and hazard-stripe markings.

I'm planning the toolkit, keeping the build around 500-700 lines, and mapping out which imports from the builder library and clockwork/glow kits I'll need for the panelled metal textures and gear details.

Now I'm sketching the skeleton: a compact ~1.35m frame with pelvis as root, a spine chain rising to the torso, skipping a jaw hinge since it's a droid rather than a creature, maybe just a vocoder grille panel on the face instead.

Rigid parts can just be placed in world-space boxes attached to bones, which keeps things simpler. For legs I'm planning sturdy two-bone limbs per side (hip, knee, ankle, foot) using a limb helper to plant the foot, with thigh and shin segments sized to land at a short ankle height.

Writing the leg chain logic...

For the side convention, s=1 maps to the left (+X), so I'll name joints L when s is positive. For the arms, I'm making them asymmetric for character: the left arm gets a standard three-finger claw gripper, while the right arm becomes a tool-arm with a welding torch, cutting disc, and drill attachment. Both rest in a slight A-pose, angled down and out from the shoulders at x=±0.30, y=1.0, using the same limb-chain approach as the legs.

I'm working out the shoulder-to-wrist geometry: placing the elbow bent slightly backward so the forearm length roughly matches the reach distance, then naming the chain joints shoulderL/elbowL/wristL with hand parts attached at the wrist, oriented along the forearm direction. For the hand itself, I'm keeping it simple—a palm box with three separated, extended fingers, each built as a short two-joint chain to avoid bloating the total joint count.

I'm reconsidering the hand design—maybe simplify so the right hand holds a tool instead of mirroring the finger rig, landing on a plan: left hand as a three-finger gripper, right hand as something distinct.

Instead I'm settling on forearm-mounted accessories for visual richness: a wrench holster and small gauge on the left forearm, and a glowing welding torch on the right forearm, while both hands still use the same three-finger builder. Now I'm working out the geometry for placing fingers around the wrist based on the forearm direction vector.

Building finger bone chains with joints for knuckles, attaching each digit's chain to the wrist joint so the hand rig parents correctly...

Now shifting to the head design -- thinking of a Star Wars droid-style dome head on a cylindrical body, with a lathe-generated dome shape and a prominent glowing photoreceptor eye.

I need to add more detail: a large central red/amber lens eye with a smaller side sensor lens, an antenna bulb, a rotating amber beacon on top, cylindrical audio sensor "ears" with grilles, and a brow visor. For the eye itself, I'm planning a lathed iris barrel ring plus a glowing textured lens disc using an SVG pattern of concentric rings and aperture blades, with emissive glow applied through the texture map.

Now I'm picking the color palette, weathered Star Wars droid style: a dingy pale cream-grey shell (#c9c4b4), safety-orange accent panels (#d9622b), gunmetal joints, and brass details. I'm also planning procedural grime paints -- mottled dirt gradients near the base, rust streaks, and carbon scoring near the torch area, built as custom paint functions blending base color with noise-based weathering.

Writing panel and metal shader logic...

Writing hazard stripe paint logic...

I'll also add wear variation using noise to darken scuffed spots, then plan out a texture list starting with a glowing eye lens.

For the rest of the texture set, I'm sketching out a secondary blue sensor lens, a chest control panel with glowing buttons and readout, faux Aurebesh decals using stylized text like "RP-77" with stencil-style glyphs, a gauge texture, a vocoder grille with horizontal slats, a caution warning triangle decal, and a spare tool rack texture.

I'm also planning a cog-emblem decal for the shoulder using the same gear texture, an ear speaker grille, hanging cable details, and a glowing power-cell bar.

Now I'm moving into the full model assembly with precise coordinates, targeting about 1.4 meters total height including the antenna, and starting with the feet design using heel blocks, toe plates, and front toe boxes to keep the geometry rigid and grounded at the floor plane.

Working out the leg geometry now, setting the ankle target height, calculating hip-to-ankle distance against segment lengths to get a natural slight knee bend, and positioning the pelvis block with hip joint cylinders rotated to align their axis correctly.

For the thighs I'm planning a rod shape with an iron core plus an outer sleeve, and adding a thin steel hydraulic piston offset slightly forward alongside the main thigh bone, running from near the hip to near the knee. Then I'll move on to building the knee joint itself.

Still shaping the knee...

For the shin I'm working out a tapered armored section using a frustum box from knee to ankle, orienting it along the world x-axis with an orange shell stripe, since dipped boxes near the floor shouldn't be an issue since the shin stops above ground level. Then I'll cap it off with a cylindrical ankle joint.

Below the ankle I'm adding an accordion-style bellows made of stacked thin cylinders as a nice droid detail, then building the foot from a box body with a tilted toe plate, heel section, and an orange top panel, keeping everything just above the floor to avoid clipping. For the torso I'm considering a barrel-like box shape with squared hips.

For the chest I'm going with a frustum-shaped box tapering from narrower hips to a wider top, plus a rectangular control panel on the front and shoulder cylinders, while the abdomen connecting pelvis to chest becomes another stack of accordion-style discs.

Adding a frame box around the panel and recalculating its front z-position based on the chest's sloped surface at that height.

I think it's more robust to use a surface ray-cast to find the exact hit point and normal on the chest, then seat the panel box along that normal so it naturally conforms to the slope, and apply the same approach for the textured decal plane.

Decals seem like the right tool for chest textures since they conform to the surface and handle lift automatically, taking a target, texture, position, direction, and size, with alpha cutouts letting the underlying color show through. I'm checking whether glow works fine on a decal's textured material — it should, since it's still just a Part — and that'll work nicely for things like glowing screen elements. Now I'm thinking about the shoulder joints, considering spheres or cylinders with orange caps and hazard-stripe detailing.

For the shoulder pads, I'm leaning toward using a lathe to create domed caps by defining a 2D outline profile and revolving it around an outward-facing axis, which gives a nice rounded shape with adjustable segments and hazard stripe coloring depending on position. For the back, I'm planning a backpack assembly with exhaust vents, cables, a tool rack with a spanner, two strapped gas canisters as vertical cylinders with domed lathe caps, and an antenna — all visible from behind — and I'm figuring out how to render the straps, possibly with torus geometry or swept loops.

Now I'm working out the hose connections: thin torus rings for straps, and catmull-rom sweeps running from the canister tops across the body to the forearm torch. Since the hoses need to stay attached to some bone, I'm deciding to anchor the first segment to the chest bone so it stays rigid, routing it over the shoulder toward the upper arm, and letting a second hose segment coil along the arm toward the torch, accepting that it'll just be correct in the rest pose rather than dynamically following the arm.

I'll go with the bone list [chest, shoulderR, elbowR] for the hose, since the docs confirm joints and chains can mix in that list.

Now I'm shaping the neck and head: placing the neck joint and accordion rods, then lathing a faceted dome head with a front plate for a dark gunmetal housing and a round eye lens.

For the head, I'm adding a secondary smaller sensor eye, side-mounted ear cylinders with grille decals, twin antennas of different heights topped with bulbs, a glowing amber beacon dome on top, and a tilted brow visor wedge above the eye.

I'm also thinking through a hinged eyelid shutter joint rigged above the lens, a textured vocoder grille plane below the eye, and back-of-head details like a vent and cable port.

Now I'm computing the face plate's exact position relative to the lathed head sphere, checking where its front corners stick out past the curved surface to create an intentional protruding visor-mask look.

Next I'm designing the eye housing as a lathed ring shape with inner/outer radii and an axial length, plus a separate flat lens circle positioned just in front to avoid z-fighting, defining the ring's profile points carefully so the outline doesn't self-intersect.

For the lens color, I'm leaning toward a warm amber-yellow glow rather than red, since the droid should read as friendly rather than menacing, using a radial gradient with a darker outer ring, bright center, dark pupil, and a small specular highlight dot.

Beyond the eyes, I want to build out the character with hazard stripes, paneled seams with rivets, a tool belt carrying a screwdriver, wrench, and hammer, clamp-lights, a shoulder floodlight, cables, and fuse cards to sell the "wow" factor. To build all this efficiently I'm sketching helper functions -- a `box` shorthand for creating box geometry parts attached to bones, and a `cyl` helper for cylinders that can be aligned along an arbitrary axis direction.

I'm also planning a `bolt` helper for small hex-head fasteners, keeping the bolt count modest (around 40) since I'm targeting roughly 300 total parts out of a 1000 limit, so merging static pieces isn't necessary yet.

Now I'm defining skeleton constants for hip, shoulder, neck, and head heights, and working out joint positions and orientations in model space to keep the coordinate system consistent rather than relying on local bone axes.

I'm setting up the joint chain from pelvis through spine, chest, neck, and head, each with position, direction, and role, making sure pelvis is the unparented root joint per the role rules. I'm also considering whether to add a jaw-like hinge joint for a chin plate or vocoder piece, even though this droid doesn't need a true jaw.

Positioning the chin vocoder plate...

Now sketching the head's lower dome and neck stack, then starting loop code to compute shoulder and wrist joint positions for the arms on both sides.

I'm using the limb function to generate joint points between shoulder and wrist, then wiring them into a chain with named joints for the shoulder, elbow, and wrist, parented to the chest -- and double-checking the reach distance makes sense for the limb lengths.

Building out the arm segments now—shoulder sphere joint, tapered rod geometry for the upper arm and forearm, with a ring accent at the elbow to give it that droid-like mechanical look.

I'm also adding a hazard-striped bracer band near the wrist and a gauge dial on the outer side of the left forearm, positioning it with an outward-facing normal so the dial reads correctly on the limb's surface.

Now I'm thinking through the right forearm torch: a barrel mounted along the forearm's front side extending past the wrist to a nozzle tip, with a small blue glowing pilot-flame cone for color. I'll also give the hands a few fingers each, with the torch sitting on top of the right hand, and I'm considering a box-shaped belt around the pelvis as a strap loop.

For the belt I'm placing a brown leather ring around the waist at the abdomen-chest junction, with a brass buckle plate, hip pouches, and hanging tools like a wrench, screwdriver, and hammer, plus maybe a small lamp on the hip. The overall torso plan is pelvis box, accordion abdomen, belt, then chest with a control panel screen and vents on front.

For the chest I'm adding a glowing blue power coupling ring, a big panel on one side and a round gauge on the other, with stenciled Aurebesh-style text. The back gets a paneled backpack box with gas canisters, a circular fan grille, and a spare-parts tool rack, while the shoulders get a glowing floodlight lens on the left and a hazard dome cap on the right, plus a stenciled unit number.

I'll skip having the hand actually hold a wrench and just hang one from the belt instead, keeping things simpler. For wiring, I'm adding coiled cable bundles in red, blue, and yellow running from the backpack to the neck, plus hydraulic hoses at the knees, all built as thin catmull sweeps, while keeping the overall flat color palette modest to stay under the color limit.

Now I'm planning the code structure, deciding to define helper functions inside the build closure so they can access the builder, and working out exactly which imports I need from the builder library and clockwork kit to avoid unused-import errors.

Writing shell paint logic...

Still writing shading logic...

Finishing the orange paint with panel seams and rivets, then wrapping it with panelling for use on tubes and boxes. I'm deciding to apply the same panelled treatment to the shell metal on large flat surfaces like the chest, backpack, and head, while keeping plain shell or a darker iron metal for small parts like fingers. Now I'm setting up the core metal palette: dark iron, tarnished steel, and brass variants.

I'm sketching a hazard-stripe paint that computes diagonal lane coordinates to alternate between yellow and dark stripes, blending in a worn grayish tone based on noise, with stripe direction varying across lathe rings. For leather I'm planning a simple grain paint using a noise-based texture between two brown tones.

Now I'm defining color constants for glow effects (amber, blue, red, warm white) and starting an SVG radial gradient for an amber lens eye texture, layering concentric rings and aperture blade lines radiating from the center...

Writing the dark pupil and highlight details...

Then I'm sketching a similar blue sensor lens texture, and designing a chest control panel texture: a dark rounded rectangle with a cyan waveform screen, colored buttons, toggle switches, and stenciled "RX-7 MAINT" lettering.

I'm planning the remaining textures too — a power gauge with a needle and "PWR" label, a circular fan grille with blades, vocoder slat lines, and a mechanic guild emblem combining a gear outline with a crossed wrench, tinted brass and painted orange on the shoulder.

I also want distressed stencil lettering like "R7-W3" in a bold Impact-style font on the chest and thigh, plus yellow warning triangles with exclamation marks on the backpack and shin, while skipping tape labels.

That's eight textures total, and decals can target any surface including swept geometry, which lets me place the chest decal directly onto the frustum sweep. Now I'm placing the pelvis geometry as a box part attached to the pelvis bone, planning to add orange hip plates, a crotch plate, and hip cylinders on each side.

Still writing cylinder helper...

Confirming flat shading won't conflict with the paint normals, then moving to leg construction — computing hip and ankle positions symmetrically for left/right sides and building limb geometry between them.

Going with the "list of one" form since the docs explicitly allow it, and I'll wire up the leg's joints so hip, knee, and ankle map cleanly from the chain's joint array with pelvis as parent.

For the leg geometry itself, I'm shaping the thigh as a rod from hip to knee bound to the hip joint, then adding a shorter, fatter orange sleeve section partway down for visual detailing.

Now I'm adding the hydraulic piston on the front of the thigh as a thin steel rod offset outward from the hip-to-knee line, bound to the same joint for animation.

Adding more joint geometry...

Still placing shin details...

For the foot, I'm shaping it as a dark box base with an orange top plate, positioning it flush with the ground so the heel sits right at floor level.

Now I'm adding a toe box piece further forward, keeping things simple by avoiding tilts or wedges and just using a plain box shape. I'm matching the ankle cylinder's bottom edge to the foot's top so the joint lines up cleanly, then adding a thin dark tread strip along the sole before moving on to pelvis and hip plate details.

Writing hip armor placement...

I'm positioning the wrench tool on the belt's front-right side, checking it won't collide with the arm, and sketching its outline shape with thickness along the depth axis.

Still plotting wrench coordinates...

Checking the wrench's position against the thigh and piston geometry to avoid collisions — it clears both at x=-0.12. I'm considering repositioning it closer to center, maybe x=-0.06, to hang more naturally between the legs.

Settling on symmetric placements: wrench at x=-0.055 and screwdriver at x=0.055, both fitting within the gap between thighs and in front of the pelvis. Now I'm working out the screwdriver's design — an orange handle cylinder with a steel shaft hanging down, tool head pointing downward.

Now I'm shifting to the chest piece, defining it as a frustum-shaped body between y=0.82 and y=1.14 with widths tapering from 0.36 to 0.26 at the base and 0.50 to 0.31 at the top, attached to the chest bone and colored with the shell material. I'm also sketching a shoulder yoke box on top, figuring out how the chest's taper at y=1.02 aligns with shoulder joints placed at x=±0.30 with a ball joint radius of 0.065.

Adding shoulder housing cylinders and collar details, then designing front chest decals—a dark bezel panel using a panel texture decal positioned near the top-left of the chest, plus a round gauge decal using a separate gauge texture placed slightly right and up from center.

I'm also planning a vent grille decal lower right, a small stencil text decal reading "R7-W3" below the panel, and a stacked three-disc neck collar between the head and chest, while skipping side vents and warning stickers for now. Writing shoulder cylinder code...

Now I'm shaping a pauldron dome over each shoulder using a lathe profile with a curved outline, colored orange and segmented for a rounded cap look, positioned to sit above the shoulder ball joint while the upper arm extends outward and down from beneath it -- checking that the dome's radius and position properly cover the joint without clipping the arm's swing.

I'm adding a hazard band ring at the dome's base using a short cylinder, plus a gear emblem decal applied to the pauldron's outer surface for detail.

A shoulder lamp goes on the chest top, built from a small housing cylinder aimed forward with a glowing lens disc and a mounting bracket. For the right shoulder I'm thinking a cable gland or antenna detail to balance the design.

For the back, I'm placing a backpack box aligned to touch the chest panel, with a paneled shell and a top-mounted fan detail.

Adding status lights...

I'm also considering exhaust stacks and gas canister details to add further mechanical texture to the backpack.

Shaping canister caps with lathe-profile domes, then adding a brass valve cylinder and small red wheel on top for the valve detail.

For hoses, I'm routing both canister lines across the backpack toward the right forearm torch: one hose arcs from the left canister valve across the back to the right shoulder and down to the elbow, following a curved path of points I'm defining through the arch, rear shoulder, and elbow positions.

For the bone ownership, the hose segment past the elbow belongs to the forearm bone, so the chain is chest → shoulderR → elbowR, with the torch resting near the forearm midpoint. Now I'm setting up hose 2, tracing the blue path from the left canister valve across the back.

I'm defining the arch and route points for hose 2, then building a reusable function to generate hose paths from a start point and intermediate route, with hose2 sharing the same route as hose1 but offset slightly along the z-axis. Writing the route coordinates...

Then I'm setting the hose radius and colors—red and blue—and adding small decorative rings along each hose at intervals using a sweep helper, constructing cylinder clips to place along the path.

Wait, actually for a sweep, the `at` point faces the outward surface normal rather than the tangent, so cylinders would end up oriented against the surface instead of along the tube. I should use a catmull path instead, which faces along the tangent — though the path itself has no bones, so it'll likely snap to the nearest joint, which could be ambiguous near the shoulder/chest boundary. I'll leave that risk for now.

I'm leaning toward building a `frame(point, direction)` manually from the path's position and tangent at a given t, then explicitly passing a bone (chest vs arm depending on t) rather than relying on nearest-joint inference. For simplicity I'll only place clips in the t range 0.15 to 0.35 and assign them to the chest bone, since that's the simplest working case.

Now I'm moving to the neck and head, setting a base head height constant and lathing a dome shape for it, considering whether to paint it with the plain shell material or the panelled variant for seam detail. I'm also sketching out a faceplate box with a bezel/visor strip rotated slightly to sit like a brow on the front of the head.

Working through the rotation math, I'm checking that a positive X-rotation of about 12 degrees tilts the brow piece downward at the front, giving it an overhanging look. I'm placing the eye centered on the face and starting to think about adding a secondary sensor element near it.

Now I'm figuring out placement for a smaller secondary lens next to the main eye, adjusting x-coordinates so the big eye ring and small lens ring don't overlap and both fit within the face plate's width, nudging the plate size slightly wider to make room.

I'm also planning additional details: tiny status LED dots below the eyes, speaker grille discs for ears made from dark cylinders with circular decal textures, and antenna rods extending upward from the top of the head toward the overall model height.

I'm placing a thin whip antenna with a small glowing red bulb tip rising to the top of the figure, and adding an amber-glowing lathe-shaped dome beacon centered on the head's crown, sitting on a dark cylindrical base.

Adding more head details now: a satellite-style dish or whip antenna offset to the side, a textured vent grille plane on the back of the head, and planning the jaw/vocoder joint position.

Still defining the lid hinge geometry...

Adjusting the eye position so the ring top lines up with the plate top, and placing the lid hinge above the eye to form a visor-like arc. I'm considering simplifying this into a lathed dome shell rather than a hand-drawn polygon shape.

Now I'm reworking the lid into a brow ridge instead: a small extruded plate positioned just above the eye, oriented along the x-axis with a thin z-depth, colored orange to match the hinge style.

Moving on to the arm geometry, I'm defining shoulder and wrist points per side and starting to build the limb between them.

Checking the arm segment distances to make sure they sum correctly, then chaining the arm bones (shoulder, elbow, wrist) under the chest parent. I'm laying out the shoulder ball joint, then building the upper arm as a tapered rod inset slightly from the joint spheres so it doesn't poke through, adding an orange sleeve section and possibly a hazard-stripe band, then moving to the elbow joint with its own sphere and connecting cylinder.

Now continuing to the forearm rod with a tapering radius toward the wrist, plus a gauntlet band and wrist ring, then building the hand: computing the wrist-to-hand direction vector and orienting a palm box along that axis, positioned just past the wrist joint.

Working out finger placement...

Still writing finger joint logic...

Now I'm sketching the hand layout: a gripper design with two fingers plus a thumb, mirrored for left and right, placing the palm base offset from the wrist and positioning each finger base relative to that point.

I'm working through the curl directions so fingers bend slightly forward while the thumb curls inward toward the fingers, creating a pincer-like grip geometry.

Now I'm placing the torch attachment on the right forearm, building its barrel, mounting clamps, tapered nozzle, and tip from cylindrical segments positioned along the forearm's forward-facing side.

I'm also adding a small blue pilot flame glow at the tip, a trigger box and gas valve at the base, and connecting hose endpoints to the torch's rear. Realizing the torch's offset could collide with the thumb at the front of the hand, I'm repositioning it to the outer side of the forearm instead, computing the outward direction based on the side sign.

For the left forearm I'm adding a gauge on the outer side, plus a small amber warning lamp beside it, placing these along the forearm sweep surface at specific angular and length positions.

Still working out the dial placement logic...

I'm sketching additional details now: a shoulder lamp on the chest, a tool rack with a diagonal probe rod and wrench on the backpack, and three colored cable loops sweeping from the chest up to the base of the head.

Rough part count totals around 250 across legs, arms, torso, head, and the back assembly. Now I'm moving on to the SVG texture strings, starting with the panel texture viewBox and rounded rectangle frame.

Writing panel SVG details...

Writing cog path function...

Still writing emblem SVG...

Adding the fan hub screws and speaker dot-grid texture, bringing the total texture count to ten: eye, sensor, panel, gauge, stencil, emblem, warn, grille, fan, and speaker. I'm also reviewing where glow effects apply across parts like the eye lens, beacon, lamp, and torch flame, checking that each material copy works correctly and that the paint check within the glow logic handles decal parts properly.

Now I'm sketching out the type definitions and helper functions for building the droid parts—defining a simple position tuple type and a box helper that wraps geometry creation with color and bone attachment options.

To keep things simple against typecheck issues, I'll type the extra options as a loose record and import `PointInput` and `DirectionInput` from the kit for position and direction, with `Joint` as the bone type. Writing cylinder helper function...

Then I'm adding smaller helpers built on top—a bolt helper that makes a hex-style brass fastener, and a ball helper for spheres—both reusing the cylinder's flat-shaded, shared-material approach, and considering using the rng for subtle scratch variations.

I decide to add surface scattering for small bolts across the backpack, filtering for near-flat-facing points and spacing them with a minimum distance, then sticking cylinder bolts at each scattered point.

Now I'm starting to draft the full build function, setting up a flat color palette for the droid's parts—rubber, leather, orange, red, blue, amber, cyan, and lamp tones—and deciding whether to define paint helpers at module scope or inside the build function.

Setting up joint hierarchy...

Setting up the leg geometry loop...

Adding knee socket and shin geometry...

Checking alignment of the orange guard against the shin surface, then working out the hazard band placement by computing the tapered shin width at that point along its length.

Now I'm defining the ankle cylinder with bolts, then building out the foot: a main shell piece, rubber sole, small top plate, and a dark toe cap.

Adding pelvis plates...

Extruding the wrench near the hip, checking its placement against the pelvis and belt front so it hangs between the thighs without clipping into them.

Now I'm adding a screwdriver hanging on the opposite side, placing its orange handle cylinder and steel shaft rod at a symmetric offset from the wrench.

I'm building the chest torso frustum shape spanning from the lower chest to the upper chest joint, then adding a flattened dark cap box at the top where the neck will attach, checking that widths stay consistent so the chest-to-neck transition looks right.

Still working out orange panel placements...

Placing more decals...

Building the neck ring cylinders and starting the lathe profile for the head dome shape.

Still positioning head geometry...

Positioning the lens circle just inside the ring and slightly above the plate, then checking the small sensor ring's radius against the big ring to see if they overlap near the edges.

I'm nudging the big eye's x-position and plate width to avoid overlap, then adding three small glow boxes beneath for the LED indicators. But checking their position shows the eye ring bottom actually overlaps below the plate edge, so I need to shift the eye upward to fix it.

Now I'm placing the LEDs to the right under the sensor instead, spacing three of them along the x-axis at a lower y-position to clear the sensor ring. Then I'm sketching the brow lid shape as an extruded arch outline with rounded smoothing, defining its orientation, thickness, and color, followed by shaping the brow overhead curve point by point.

I'm checking that the brow arch doesn't clash with the ring and lens positions vertically and that it sits as a protruding visor in front of the dome's silhouette rather than tucked inside it—it ends up as a fairly tall hood shape given the vertical extent of the points.

I'm reducing the arch height values to soften the brow for a more "curious" rather than aggressive look. Then I move to the ears, defining a dark cylinder for the ear housing plus a speaker grille circle and an orange ear-cup ring, oriented to face outward along the side axis, followed by setting up the beacon, antennas, and a rear head vent, and finally sketching a lathe profile for a small satellite-dish shape with a thin shell outline pointing upward.

Fixing the dish outline into a proper closed polygon and tilting its lathe axis toward the front-left, normalizing that direction vector manually, then mounting it on a stalk below the head. Moving on to the backpack, I'm placing blue and red canisters symmetrically on either side of the chest, adding a central pack box with a dark top cap, and starting on exhaust stack cylinders mounted near the top of the pack.

Still placing cylinder tanks...

Adding bottom shoe strap at y 0.77, then designing a worn paint function that blends a base color with dark grime using noise for a weathered canister look.

Now I'm planning to build the arm points, elbows, and hose paths into a record structure before adding back-mounted tools like a spare rod and wrench.

I'm positioning the diagonal rod so it crosses the backpack without overlapping the fan decal, adjusting coordinates to keep the strap-across-pipe look readable.

Adjusting the pipe bracket position lower on the back, then considering adding a small coiled cable using the kit's coil-path helper to sweep a thin spring shape between two back points, similar to how a leg shock spring might be built.

I'm thinking about wrapping a coil spring around the thigh piston path for visual detail, estimating triangle counts for the sweep geometry across both legs and checking it fits within the overall budget, possibly reducing side count to keep it efficient.

I'll skip adding extra details like cables, repair lamps, and exposed wiring panels for now to keep things simple, and move on to confirming the root centering of the model.

Writing hand geometry logic...

Since width axis maps closer to the "out" direction, I'm placing fingers at ±out offsets for side-by-side spread, with the thumb along fwd for the pinch gesture. For the palm I'm using a dark box with a small orange plate on the back for the knuckle guard detail.

I'm second-guessing which side counts as the hand's back since the plate's local thickness axis might not line up with fwd, risking misplacement if orientation isn't handled carefully — I'm considering using the `up` parameter to pin the roll explicitly rather than relying on a raw directional offset.

Setting `up: fwd` so the local axes align properly for the back plate, then positioning the fingers by spreading them outward from the palm base with slightly different offsets for index, middle, and thumb.

Now I'm working out finger curl directions and lengths — fingers curl toward the thumb side while the thumb curls backward toward center — assigning segment lengths and radii, then structuring the joint hierarchy as a parent chain.

I'm also positioning the torch and hoses attached near the elbow/forearm, placing the barrel offset from the forearm axis and matching its radius to the forearm's tapered surface.

Still writing torch geometry...

Checking clearance between finger width and torch barrel, then sizing forearm bracket cylinders to taper slightly larger than the forearm radius. I'm setting up storage for right-arm data like shoulder/elbow joints and torch rear point so I can route hoses afterward.

Mapping out the hose path from a fixed anchor point near the back, offsetting from the shoulder joint behind the body, then following the upper arm direction toward the elbow with a backward offset before connecting to the torch rear point.

Still defining path points...

The frame bone option checks out fine. Moving to the pauldron: I'll lathe a domed outline outward along the shoulder axis with radius 0.095, plus a hazard-striped ring placed at its base.

Now I'm checking overlap — the hazard ring at x=0.34 sits right against the dome base at 0.335, and the emblem decal placed on the dome surface at [0.405, 1.04, 0] reads fine, with the dome apex extending to about 0.42. The dark shoulder housing cylinder at x=0.27 with radius 0.085 and length 0.11 covers 0.215 to 0.325, overlapping into the chest side appropriately.

For the arm, the upper segment starts at the shoulder joint around (0.30, 1.02, 0), with the sleeve beginning underneath the pauldron at roughly y=0.95 so it peeks out from under the shoulder cap correctly.

Now I'm designing a small shoulder lamp on the left side of the chest around (0.15, 1.17, 0.09) — a dark cylindrical base, a tapered barrel angled forward and slightly upward, and a glowing circular lens on the front face, making sure it fits within the chest's front edge and clears the neck geometry. For the right shoulder, I'm considering adding a small decorative element like a fuse rack with a few glass fuse cylinders.

Then I'm placing three small fuse-cartridge cylinders near x -0.15 to -0.19, glowing amber, red, and green, and adding a hazard-striped band across the chest's bottom edge sized slightly larger than the torso's footprint.
